Global Economic Environment
The global macroeconomic landscape became 
increasingly challenging in early 2026 following 
the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East. 
Disruptions to energy supplies and key trade routes 
led to increased volatility in energy prices, freight 
rates and logistics costs. The sharp increase in 
memory prices was a global, industry-wide macro 
trend, driven by supply rationalisation, capacity 
constraints and strong demand from AI/data centres, 
rather than company-specific factors.
Global Real GDP Growth Trend (%)
According to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in 
its July 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO) Update, 
global GDP growth is projected to slow down to 3.0% 
in 2026, before recovering to 3.4% in 2027. Although 
risks to the outlook have become more balanced 
compared with early 2026, uncertainty continues 
to remain elevated. Any renewed geopolitical 
escalation, commodity price volatility, financial 
market repricing or persistent inflationary pressures 
could weigh on global economic growth.

Indian Economic Environment
Amid an uncertain global economic environment, 
India continued to be the world’s fastest-growing 
major economy during 2025–26, supported by 
strong domestic demand, sustained public capital 
expenditure and a gradual recovery in private 
investment. As per the revised national accounts 
series with 2022–23 as the base year, the country’s 
real GDP is estimated to have expanded by 7.7%, while 
real Gross Value Added (GVA) grew by 7.9%.
Global Electronics Industry
The electronics industry comprises the design, 
manufacture and sale of electronic equipment and 
components. It supports a wide range of sectors, 
including consumer electronics, automotive, 
telecommunications, healthcare, aerospace and 
industrial automation. The global electronics market 
is undergoing a dynamic transformation, driven by 
rapid technological advancements and evolving 
consumer expectations. From the rise of AI and smart 
devices to a growing emphasis on sustainability, the 
industry continues to innovate to meet changing 
market demands. Valued at around US$ 2.3-2.4 
Trillion in CY 2025, the global electronics industry is 
projected to reach US$ 4.4-4.5 Trillion by CY 2035, 
growing at a CAGR of 6.2% over the period. While the 
opportunities are significant, the sector also faces 
challenges arising from supply chain complexities 
and an evolving regulatory landscape. Even so, the 
electronics industry remains one of the fastest-
growing and most dynamic sectors globally.

Evolving Scope of EMS Capabilities
EMS providers support customers across multiple stages of the product lifecycle, with the breadth of services 
varying by scale and capabilities. While large EMS companies offer end-to-end solutions spanning product 
design, component sourcing, manufacturing, testing and after-sales support, smaller and mid-sized players 
typically focus on manufacturing, assembly and testing services.

Key Market Restraints
 Supply chain vulnerabilities arising from material 
shortages, geopolitical uncertainties, logistics 
disruptions and natural disasters can impact 
component availability, extend lead times and 
increase operating costs.
 Regulatory compliance is becoming increasingly 
complex, with EMS providers required to adhere 
to diverse safety, labour, environmental and trade 
regulations across multiple jurisdictions.
 Intellectual property risks remain a key concern as 
increasing outsourcing requires EMS providers to 
implement robust legal, cybersecurity and data 
protection measures.
 Intense market competition continues to exert 
pricing pressure, as the presence of a large 
number of EMS providers across geographies limits 
pricing power and impacts revenue potential.
 Skilled talent availability remains a critical 
concern, with increasing competition for 
experienced engineering, R&D, technical and sales 
professionals contributing to talent shortages and 
higher attrition.

Business Performance Review
2025-26 was a year of strong financial performance 
and significant strategic progress for us, despite 
an increasingly challenging external environment. 
We delivered consolidated revenue¹ of ₹48,893 
Crores (excluding exceptional gain), up 26% YoY, 
while EBITDA¹ excluding exceptional gain increased 
23% to ₹1,887 Crores and PAT excluding exceptional 
gain increased 20% to ₹845 Crores. Importantly, we 
maintained strong financial and operating discipline, 
with ROCE² of 44.8%, ROE of 28.1% and a negative 
working-capital cycle³ of 8 days, reflecting healthy 
capital efficiency, strong cash-flow generation and 
balance-sheet discipline. 
At the same time, the year was marked by several 
external headwinds. The electronics industry 
experienced significant inflation in key components, 
particularly memory chips and semiconductor-
linked inputs, driven in part by AI and data-centre 
demand, which led to supply constraints and higher 
input costs for traditional consumer electronics. 
The latter part of the year was also impacted by 
geopolitical tensions, supply-chain and freight 
disruptions, energy and commodity-price volatility, 
currency movements, softer consumer demand and 
inventory rationalisation by brands, with smartphones 
and IT Hardware being particularly affected. These 
factors resulted in a more cautious procurement 
environment among customers and moderated 
growth in some of our businesses. 
Despite these near-term challenges, we remained 
focused on strengthening customer partnerships, 
expanding capacities, improving operational 
efficiency and accelerating our backward integration 
and localisation strategy. We continued to invest 
in critical components such as camera modules, 
display modules and optical transceivers, while 
expanding our manufacturing footprint across Mobile, 
Telecom, IT Hardware, Home Appliances and other 
segments. We also continued to invest in talent 
and capability enhancement, with the objective 
of strengthening our competitive positioning and 
increasing the value addition captured within India. 
Overall, we believe the underlying fundamentals of 
our business remain strong, and our low leverage, 
healthy return ratios, negative working-capital 
cycle and strong balance sheet provide us with 
the flexibility to invest through the cycle. We 
remain confident in the long-term India electronics 
manufacturing opportunity, supported by global 
supply-chain diversification, increasing localisation, 
supportive government policies and PLI/ECMS-led 
investments, and believe these structural factors 
provide Dixon with a strong multi-year runway for 
sustainable and profitable growth.

capital and returns. We are conscious that the

electronics manufacturing in India.
